title: The ONLY Way to Build a $1M+ SaaS in 2026
normalization: Concatenate utf8 segments per caption event; retain event start and duration; whitespace trim only.

segments.text: It's 2026 and most SaaS founders are
going to fail this year. CAC is up, LTV
is down, anything that gets traction is
copied in 60 days, and buyers don't
trust anyone anymore. Now, over the last
decade, I bootstrapped three SaaS
companies to a combined 35 million ARR,
and right now I'm watching a lot of
smart founders sprint in the wrong
direction. But, the good news is
building a seven-to-eight-figure startup
today is still entirely possible, and
that's why in this video I'm breaking
down the seven things I'm personally
doing or things I've seen people do
close [music] to me that actually work
when it comes to scaling a SaaS. The
number one is creating a truly AI-first
startup. Most founders think they're
building an AI company when they're
really just using AI as a feature.
There's a big difference between
slapping some LLMs on top of your
existing workflow and actually building
something that couldn't have existed two
years ago. The first is incremental, the
second is a completely new category. The
companies actually growing right now are
using AI as the foundation of the
product, not a layer on top. Cursor and
Windserf are obvious examples. They
didn't add AI to a code editor, they
built an entire product around what AI
has made possible. The result is a
tenfold productivity gain for the user,
which is why people can't stop talking
about them. The question you need to ask
about your own product is, does using it
make someone 10 times more productive
than before? If the answer isn't a clear
yes, you're not truly AI-first. And if
you're not truly AI-first in 2026,
with the same playing field as everyone
else, which means you're competing on
CAC, and that is a race you're probably
losing. Number two is word of mouth.
This one's always mattered, but in 2026
it's more critical than ever, and here's
the specific way I think about it. If
you have strong word of mouth,
everything else you do works. If you
don't have word of mouth, nothing you do
works. It's that binary. Word of mouth
is really just another word for product
market fit. It's when you built the
right product for the right buyers at
the right time. When it clicks, it's
obvious. People are sharing your product
on social without you asking them to,
prospects are saying, "I heard about you
from XYZ customer," and customers would
be furious if you took the product away.
And if you did nothing, you would still
see organic growth. Number three is
personal brand. If you're a founder and
you're not building a personal brand
today, you're leaving a lot on the
table. The ability to create organic
content that your target market actually
wants, completely independent of what
you're selling, is the most efficient
go-to-market motion that has ever
existed. It's an automated
trust-building machine, and trust is
brand. [music] I went from 4,000 to
150,000 LinkedIn followers in 24 months,
and I used that audience to take RB2B
from zero to 1 million ARR in just six
weeks. My LinkedIn content generates
more qualified pipeline than my
20-person sales team at retention.com, a
team that costs $2.65 million per year.
Now, here's what most founders get wrong
about building a personal brand. They
try to sound like a big professional
company. They only share wins, they
avoid being vulnerable because they're
worried about what competitors will
think, and that is exactly the opposite
of what works. My breakthrough came from
a massive failure. In 2023, I made a big
bet and I lost. I publicly predicted we
would nearly triple retention.com's
revenue from 15 to 45 million ARR.
Instead, we barely moved the needle at
40% growth, and I had to cut the entire
BDR team after our outbound strategy
fell apart. The people around me thought
I should stay quiet, that sharing it
publicly would just hand ammunition to
competitors. But, I put it all out there
anyway, the miss, the layoffs, the
actual numbers. And what happened next
is the reason I talk about personal
brand so much. Other B2B founders were
going through the same thing, and nobody
was talking about it. That transparency
created the most engaged audience I've
ever built. And when I launched RB2B,
the people already felt like they knew
me. The reason this works is simple.
Your content creates a human-to-human
connection scale that a paid ad simply
cannot replicate. Large companies have
to pay for these impressions. For a
founder with a personal brand, it's
free. Now, if you're building a personal
brand on LinkedIn and using it as part
of your go-to-market, there's one thing
I'd add on top of it. Most of the time,
people visit your website after seeing
your content, and they just disappear.
You have no idea who they are. That's
where RB2B comes in. We identify your
anonymous website visitors at the person
level, their full name, job title,
LinkedIn profile, and business email,
and we send that directly to your Slack
in real time. These are your warmest
leads because they already know who you
are from your content, and they're
actively looking at your site. If you
want to start using this for free, just
click the link below. Let's go to the
fourth thing on this list of strategies
that work today. Number four is cold
email, but only in specific contexts. I
want to be clear on this. Very
knowledgeable people in the cold email
space like Jesse Willat are reporting
their blocking enterprise buyers
completely. It just doesn't work there.
If you're selling to SMB or VC-backed
startups, there's still real money here,
and at RB2B, cold email generates around
20% of our revenue still. So, the people
telling you cold email is dead are just
doing it wrong. The most common mistake
founders make with cold email is
focusing on the message before sorting
out the infrastructure. Your perfect
email means nothing if it lands in a
spam folder. Most founders don't even
realize their emails aren't getting
delivered. And on copy, what works is
keeping it short, direct, and written
like a DM to a friend, not a marketing
email. Most cold emails are like, "Hey,
first name, I exist, you exist, can I
take 15 minutes of your time?" Or worse,
people are using AI to write
personalized first lines, and everyone
reading them knows immediately that
they're AI-generated. But, if you're
writing an email to the right list with
the right copy, it can be a very
profitable growth channel. Number five
are thought leadership ads. If you're
already posting on LinkedIn and some of
your content's performing well, this is
the easiest money you're probably
leaving on the table. The idea is
straightforward. Take your
best-performing organic post and put
some ad spend behind them. LinkedIn
thought leadership ads let you promote a
post you already know the platform
loves, and you have proof of concept
before you even spend a dollar. That
makes it one of the cheapest sources of
new eyeballs you can get because you're
not guessing whether the content works.
The key is that it only works if the
organic content is already strong. You
can't boost mediocre posts and expect a
different outcome. But, if you know how
to create posts that consistently get
strong engagement, picking the best ones
and putting money behind them is a
pretty obvious move. Number six is cold
calls. Most people roll their eyes at
cold calling in 2026, but honestly,
that's exactly why it's working again.
Everyone moved from cold calling to
LinkedIn DMs, but the phone is actually
less crowded right now than it has been
in years. I recently talked to one of my
good friends, Kevin Dorsey, on my
podcast, and we walked through the exact
script his team's running right now. The
results they see from this are pretty
insane. He said there's a 12-to-13% rate
of accepting the pitch on 200 dials per
day per rep. That's booking 20 to 25
meetings per week per rep. One
well-trained rep running the right
script can generate over 80 meetings a
month. So, cold calling is silently
becoming one of the best channels again
today. Staying ridiculously lean is
number seven. This is the one that ties
everything else together because all of
the tactics above are meaningless if you
burn out or run out of money chasing the
wrong metrics. The companies I see
winning right now are running tiny
teams, staying profitable, and
controlling their own destiny. Getting
to 10 million ARR with under 10 people
is now the gold standard, not raising a
100 million round at a unicorn
valuation. I learned the hard way at
retention.com. We hit product market
fit, and I thought I was ready to scale,
so I hired 50 people in 60 days. Things
that took two hours at 1 million ARR
with two people suddenly took two weeks.
I was spending 60% of my time on
internal meetings and hiring instead of
talking to customers and improving the
product. That's the dust pile. The
person who's the best at marketing, the
best at product, and the best at
go-to-market is spending most of their
time not doing any of those things. On
the other hand, my newest SaaS, RB2B, is
almost at 8 million ARR, and we only
have three full-time employees. We move
fast because we have fewer things to do.
100% of my time goes toward making the
product better and talking to customers.
Here's why lean is also the right
financial decision. At 10 million ARR
with a small and efficient team, you and
your co-founder can each clear over a
million a year, maybe 2 million in
salary and dividends. You could sell
that company right now for 40 to 50
million if you want to, and there are
thousands of buyers for a profitable 10
million ARR business. With VC money, you
don't get to make that call. You're
waiting for someone else's exit on
someone else's timeline. Now, having
said all of this, one thing's true.
Buyers in 2026 don't trust anything they
haven't already encountered before. Cold
ads from brand they've never heard of,
cold emails from a stranger, cold calls
from someone they have no context on,
none of it lands the way it used to.
Founders winning right now have figured
out that you need to create familiarity
before you try to sell anything.
Personal brand does that at scale. Word
of mouth does it organically. Even cold
email works better when the person on
the other end has already seen your
[music] content. That's exactly why I
built RB2B. Most of the people visiting
your website already have some level of
awareness of you. They came from
somewhere, but 97% of them leave without
doing anything, and you have no idea who
they were. RB2B identifies those
visitors at the person level, their
name, job title, LinkedIn profile, and
business email, and sends them straight
to your Slack so you can follow up while
they're still warm. If you want to try
right now, just click the first link in
the description. And if you want to see
what my days look like running two SaaS
companies with over 30 million ARR
combined, then watch this video next.
